title: Deficits and Debt
objective: After this level you can explain government deficits and debt.
summary: A deficit is spending above revenue in a year; borrowing to cover deficits builds debt. The IMF expects global public debt to pass 100% of GDP by 2029. Views on limits differ.

cards.headline: Global public debt is heading for its highest level since 1948.
cards.body: That's the IMF's projection: government debt worldwide rising above 100% of world GDP by 2029. How does a government end up owing more than a year's worth of everything its economy produces? One year at a time.

cards.headline: The yearly gap
cards.body: Level 71's budget has two sides. When spending beats revenue, the gap is a deficit; the reverse is a surplus. To cover a deficit, a government borrows, mostly by selling bonds: 79.3% of OECD public debt takes that form. Run deficits year after year and they pile up as debt.

cards.fact: In 2023, only six OECD countries ran a surplus.
cards.context: The average OECD government ran a deficit of 4.6% of GDP. Norway led the small surplus club at 16.5%.

cards.headline: Big debts, different risks
cards.body: Among the G20, Canada, China, France, Italy, Japan, the UK and the US have debts above 100% of GDP, or soon will. The IMF rates their risk as moderate, thanks to deep markets for their bonds. Meanwhile 55 countries are in or near debt distress, often with debts below 60%. The size of a debt isn't the whole story; its cost matters too.

mascot.line: Owing a lot isn't the same as being in trouble. A debt's size isn't the whole story; its cost matters too.

cards.headline: How much debt is too much? Three answers

items.label: The OECD
points: Sustainable deficits can fund public investment
And cushion recessions, pandemics and disasters

items.label: Germany's rule
points: A 'debt brake' caps the structural deficit at 0.35% of GDP
Since 2025, defence above 1% of GDP is exempt

cards.headline: Debt: explained
learned: Deficit: spending above revenue in a year
Borrowing to cover deficits builds debt
IMF: global debt above 100% of GDP by 2029
The IMF, the OECD and Germany's rule differ on limits

questions.prompt: In a government's yearly accounts, when is the fiscal balance a deficit?

options.label: When spending is greater than revenue
When revenue is greater than spending
When the debt has been fully repaid
options.rationale: Repaying debt doesn't define a yearly deficit.

options.label: When taxes are cut to zero
options.rationale: A deficit is about spending versus revenue, whatever the tax level.

questions.explanation: The fiscal balance is revenue minus spending; when spending is greater, it's a deficit.

questions.prompt: Why does the IMF rate the fiscal risk of high-debt G20 countries like Japan as only moderate?

options.label: Their debts are secretly small
options.rationale: Their debts are above, or near, 100% of GDP.

options.label: They never borrow abroad
options.rationale: The IMF's reason is the depth of their bond markets.

options.label: They have deep, liquid markets for their bonds
Their debts don't charge interest
options.rationale: Government debt carries interest; cost matters.

questions.explanation: Deep, liquid bond markets and broad policy choices mean the IMF sees their fiscal risk as moderate despite debts above 100% of GDP.

questions.prompt: Level 6 called taxes compulsory payments to government. When spending runs ahead of that revenue, what does a government do?

options.label: Raises every tax automatically
options.rationale: Nothing makes taxes rise by themselves; the gap is borrowed.

options.label: Stops all spending until next year
options.rationale: Governments keep spending and borrow the gap.

options.label: Declares a surplus to cover it
options.rationale: A surplus is when revenue beats spending.

questions.explanation: Spending above revenue is a deficit, and governments borrow to cover it, mostly by selling bonds; year after year the borrowing piles up as debt.
